utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, you asked to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly. In connection with the Court's inquiry into the Nielsen materials and requests that the parties confer in an attempt to resolve that, I spoke with Mr. Stewart this morning, advised him that the Prosecution had prepared two binders, one containing, A, reports to the Presidency; B, reports to the government; and C, daily bulletins, referring to mopping-up or detention facilities; and another binder which contained all the additional daily bulletins. Because of his schedule, Mr. Stewart and I were unable to confer personally but by telephone, but he was making arrangements to pick up the binders to -- for the purpose of viewing them. And I indicated to him I would advise the Court of our discussion and the status of our efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I looked again in the transcript of what we said about this material, and I think at that time we said that if one of the parties would like to -- to introduce this material, that of course the Chamber would -- would accept that but not necessarily ask for it at that moment. The Chamber feels some need to - as we always try to do - to find an objective basis which allows us to verify conclusions because very often conclusions are thought -- until now the Defence has not asked for it, so that suggests that the Defence was satisfied with the conclusions, at least that they did not ask for any further material to verify that. The Chamber is not saying that it will go through all of this material, but just to have at least an opportunity to check whether the type of material justifies the conclusions drawn. The Chamber will wait and see what the results of your further discussions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, if there's no other procedural issue, Mr. Josse, I think for next Monday it's better to wait and see what happens today so that we have a better impression of what pace we can keep up and then see whether there's any need to further decide on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as you suggested. Yes, then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Radojko into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your "dobar dan," I take it you can hear me in a language you understand. Mr. Radojko, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse will now continue his re-examination. Mr. Josse, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be given P64A, binder 11, footnote 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for ease of reference, is that one of the items tabbed for this particular witness; and if so, which tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 4. And could the witness turn to page 177 in his version, page 101 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see here, Mr. Radojko, your notes of the 1st of July of 1992, and at some point, maybe on page 178 in your version, we see that you have written: "What if they don't find anything to exchange. Two possibilities: Staying, leaving without guarantees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, I'm looking, the keyboard of your case manager sounds very loud in -- no, no, I don't want you to stop working, but I wondered whether there was a microphone open closer to the keyboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I've got the -- I'm using the one furthest away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Karganovic, if you would put your earphones on, you would hear how loud it approximately is. But I do not want you to -- perhaps another place would -- okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have the passage I'm referring to, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then it goes on and says: "Attitude of the authorities: They do not want an ethnically pure area, but the pressures are strong." Which authorities are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they're talking about here are the local authorities. I don't know which other authorities this could refer to. The notes partly served as a reminder to me because somebody mentioned Jasna Karanovic in connection with Zecevic and I recall that this Zecevic was an Ustasha, and it says here: "Rajko will send her over." And I recall the problems which had to do with the exchanges. I kept drawing their attention to the fact that this could entail a series of legal issues and that this should not be done chaotically. Secondly, it says here: "Contracts. Legal validity, validity of legal basis," and I said that -- this refers to the fact that I was drawing their attention to the fact that there were no legal bases for that and that people being sent for exchanges. This was a framework that was already problematic at the time and it was not to be implemented. This -- it says here: "We don't want an ethnically clean area, but the pressure is strong." Probably the president told me what the reason was behind such a request.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Zecevic was not an Ustasha; rather a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that I ought to have presented the problem to the representatives of the Muslim community because it says here that the Muslim community should be contacted on the issue of their property and so on and so forth. And I was probably, by making these notes, trying to prepare myself for this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when it refers to "pressures are strong," what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was common knowledge. The pressure came - I'm not sure whether it was the members of the army who exerted pressure - but it was the representative of the command who kept telling us that they did not want -- that the Muslims did not want to become members of the army, that they did not wish to have them there, and this was the sort of pressure that existed. We had various ad hoc delegations arriving at the municipality because probably several members of a military unit, five, six, or seven, would form a group and then approach the president, telling him that they would not allow for the situation to continue as such, that they would themselves take care of matters, and so on and so forth. And I myself perceived it as pressure exerted on the local authorities. I believe the others did as well. Besides, I was not the person who represented the municipal authorities before these people; it was those others. I was there merely as a person who would take a note or two, but they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm just -- the witness mentioned a couple of times - I couldn't find that - "the validity of the contracts."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm -- well, perhaps we -- I could make an assumption and a guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be far more desirable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you -- I have not found yet the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, the learned Judge would like to know about your reference to the validity of the contracts. Is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I perhaps -- I read it. It says here: "Contracts, legal validity, validity of legal basis." I did not find that right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is that a reference to in your diary, Mr. Radojko?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But first I would like to find it. Is it on page 101? What page is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Direct us to the reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- for that remark. Read out the words you were looking at when you made that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my version that's on page 178 or 179 of this diary, as we call it. Page 178, that's the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And read out the words, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are notes, and the first one reads: "Legal remedy in laesio enormis." The second one is: "Validity of legal basis." The third entry: "What to do with the people who will not leave." The fourth entry: "What if nothing is found for the exchange?" And then there are two possibilities, that: "Someone stays or leaves without any guarantees." Fourth entry: "Attitude of the authorities that they don't want an ethnically pure area, but the pressures are strong." That's what the entries say. As far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first -- because there was a part illegible for the translators at the time. You said legal remedy in case of -- and I think you say "laesio enormis." Can you explain that, although it sounds, in my legal mind, Latin for "major disadvantage" or "major damage."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're right. It wasn't written correctly here, though, because I -- it says, in fact, "legal remedy." And I may note that there was the possibility of the so-called excessive prejudice -- or rather, excessive damage, that's to say, not prejudice. And that would mean more than half of damage to a property is done. For instance, if someone, out of $100, loses $60, then this would place him in such a disadvantageous position, and that's why a contract which, let's say, regulates something like that would be invalid. I wanted to point out to the fact that there were difficulties with the time limits in the context of the departure of the people. I wanted to draw their attention to all the possible difficulties arising from this to the best of my knowledge. I went through all the different contracts, and I felt that by first making copies of contracts and then letting people to fill them out was the improper way of approaching this, and I was drawing their attention to this as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you: How many people signed the contracts for exchange of property? Approximately how many of these contracts were concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't involved in this work and I can't give you a precise answer. When I asked some of the people who kept records there, there were between 110 and 130 of them. I seem to have this figure of 130-odd in my mind, but it doesn't necessarily mean that the -- this is the exact figure. Maybe this is just the feeling that I have. But very soon the practice was discontinued, or maybe the persons involved were no longer interested in exchanging their properties. The situation changed day-in, day-out. The people from Bihac were exchanging their property for other properties, and very soon they realised that the property in Petrovac was not worth that much as property over there in Bihac, and that's why they stopped doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many people would have donated their immovable property to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know that. I don't think the numbers are high, though. Very soon people realised that such a transfer of property had no legal validity, and besides, the party that was taking the property into their care only assumed too much responsibility upon their shoulders; that's why they stopped the practice. In the municipal archives there must be reference numbers, and I believe that if someone were to go over there and review the archives would be able to find every single one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radojko, just from point of view of logic, would you please respond to the following: If people would think that a donation contract would be legally valid, I would expect them to be hesitant to sign it because they would lose their property. As soon as people realise that it's not legally valid, I would say that they have less problems in signing it - isn't that logical? - whereas you seem to use an opposite logic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There wasn't that much interest on either side to conclude such contracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about donations. I'm not talking about exchange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, you mean donations. Well, from the very start not only I but all the other lawyers pointed to their deficiencies, and this wasn't something that the people didn't know about. I think the overwhelming majority of people knew that this was null and void, and I mean those who were donating their property. But there were, of course, instances of people who reconciled with the situation, gave their property away, and probably knew that this would, in time, turn out to be invalid. I'm sure that they had people to turn to. There were lawyers on -- among Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, wasn't it a bit the world upside down; the Crisis Staff deciding that they should donate their property and then people seeking advice from lawyers - I can imagine that under those circumstances seeking advice from a lawyer, which isn't a pleasant thing to do anyhow, that people might have had other things on their mind - and then to say: We sought advice from lawyers, they tell us that it's not valid anyway, so let's not sign it, where the Crisis Staff had decided they had to sign it. And from this advice, they would have learned that there was no risk in signing it because it would be invalid anyhow. So why not meet what the Crisis Staff asked? I have some difficulties in following the logic of it all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe your understanding of the logic is quite correct: The world was, in fact, upside down. We had lawyers, but not those admitted to the bar, not the practicing lawyers in those terms, but this was a small town. Now, let me illustrate this situation. The president of the Executive Board left significant property behind in Bihac, that of his and his family. I drafted a contract for him on the exchange of property with a man by the name Barjaktarevic who was among the people who wanted to leave the area with the international assistance. On that occasion during their conversation, which I was able to hear -- the name of the other man is Bahtijaragic. They, as they spoke about it, knew that it was invalid and were actually saying that they had the intention of taking care of one other's property. All the other staff in the municipality were aware of the fact this did not carry any weight. By the time they produced a contract and signed it, they knew it would amount to nothing, that it wouldn't have any valid meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've slowly moved back to the exchange again, but -- apart from that -- well, we've carefully listened to your explanation. Would there be -- because I don't think, Mr. Tieger, did we ever receive any contracts on exchange of property or did we just receive the -- I wouldn't call it "contracts" but the declaration of donating the property to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just the latter, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it would perhaps assist the Chamber to be able to compare the -- even if we have no exact information about what numbers of exchange contracts or what numbers of donation documents were there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the witness said that one could find examples of these today in his municipality - I'm trying to find the passage but can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he said so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- it crossed my mind at that point in time whether that was part of the task that Mr. Harmon's investigators are undertaking at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, we asked for the other type of contracts, not having been informed in a similar way about the exchange. And what surprises me a bit, the witness tells us that these exchange contracts, which in my first impression could have -- could have contributed to a resolution of an urgent problem for those who were about to leave and those who would stay, that I did not ab initio consider them to be illegal. At least, I have no information that they were considered to be without any effect and illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I say this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is no prospect of the Defence getting hold of this material, for logistical reasons, plain and simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like you to go back a little and look at this document again. We can read: "Attitude of the authorities: They do not want an ethnically pure area but the pressures are strong." I would like you to comment that again, please, "but the pressures are strong." You said that the pressure came primarily from the military. Could you take it a little further and could you tell me what kind of pressure this was. What did the military want and what was their objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer your question. I've already told you that this representative of the Crisis Staff, who spoke on behalf of the army, gave very firm and radical requests to that effect, saying that he was speaking on behalf of the army. And he did so on several occasions. First, they asked for the Muslims to be mobilised because they dodged call-ups, and then there were requests for them to be forced to perform work obligation. Once they wanted to use them to clear up a road to facilitate passage of the army. They insisted that they be given work obligation, which was like a military duty but the person would be given civilian jobs instead. When a good many Muslims agreed to such a work obligation, then the representatives said: Well, why should we be the one to wage the war and risk our lives and they not? So the army did not have a clear objective or strategy vis-a-vis the Muslims. Then the Muslim representatives would come up and threaten the municipal staff and tell us: You should mind what you're doing or else we will have our say. There was this one instance when an entire battalion opened fire, not at the municipal building itself but around the building; and this was an entire battalion of some 700 people. And you can imagine how that must have been. I wasn't away; I was in my unit at the time, but I heard about the situation. Then, for instance, they would enter the municipal premises armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau, would you mind speaking into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence you've written in your nobody is quite clear. "They do not want an ethnically pure area, but the pressures are strong," it seems to indicate that pressures are strong because an ethnically pure area should be created. So this is my question: Did the army, by its representatives, clearly indicate that it wanted an area or part of the country to be ethnically pure? I'm not talking about work or something like that which the Muslims had to perform. You say: "My local authorities don't want an ethnically pure area, but the pressures are strong," this seems to indicate that the pressure is very strong to make sure that this ethnically pure area is created. Was this something that was actually said in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something like that was never said, but this sort of conduct where you ask people to do one thing and then once they implement what you ask, then they ask you to do something else, then there's no end to this. The only conclusion can be that they wanted the people to be moved out of the area. That's my understanding of it. This has been a long time ago, and I've been through many other things since then, but that was the state of affairs. They were told to perform work obligation, and then when they do, then they are again attacked. They don't want to have them at home, they want them to clear the roads. When they start clearing the roads, then they are exposed to threats or even worse. Then the question is raised as to why they're not doing anything out in the streets. You can see that they were not satisfied with these people. This particular note was to serve as a reminder for something to be done. I don't recall now whether a document, an order was to be drawn up on the basis of this or something else, but I'm simply recounting you the state of affairs as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you next turn to page 100 -- 213, please. In the English, 120. We see that these are your notes of a session of the Executive Committee dated the 21st of July of 1992. We see various conclusions, and there are two different matters I wish to ask you about. The first follows on from what you have just been giving evidence about. It says: "Conclusion: Records of all humanitarian aid to be kept through a general list in order to have an overall insight ... "J. Sepa:m. no longer wish to exchange real estate. Permits for moving out have not been issued ... Muslims would sign contracts only once they set off from here ..." What does that mean, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've actually answered this already. This attempt was a very short-lived one, that is to say, returning properties or exchanging properties, and that is why these permits for moving out were not issued, because there weren't enough people interested in that. Otherwise, the number that you're referring to is 66, so there weren't that many -- well, not contracts but statements. Perhaps there were even less contracts than statements. You see that this was done within those services there, and Muslims should sign contracts only when they leave. So that is only when they will sign these contracts. They don't want to sign these contracts and stay there. You know, if they had signed contracts and stayed there, their fate would be pretty uncertain, and they had exchanged their property, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next line read: "Bogdan: Proposes police be informed about every case of forceful occupation of flats ... There can be no unfounded occupation of property, otherwise they have to be evicted ... "Adopted as a conclusion."

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases that these people who had fled from Bihac started entering other people's houses, Muslim houses for the most part -- well, most often it was Muslim houses, yes. So there would be the main building and then another building within the same compound. Some would be empty, but they would just barge in, move in. Well -- because in that area there wasn't enough space for people to live in, so they also started taking up Muslim businesses. They wanted to get them out of their shops and they wanted to report these people who had entered their shops by force to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if you look at page 224, the 9th of August, 126 in the English, we see a note of the Petrovac War Presidency, 46th Session. Number 2: "Prevention of unauthorised occupation of abandoned property." Is that the same point?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same point, the same point. There were Muslim families, for instance, that, for the sake of some kind of safety and security, if somebody were living on their own, they'd move to live with their children or relatives. And then once their apartment would be abandoned, then somebody else would move into that apartment; that kind of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you next turn to page 236 in the original, 133 in our translations, which is your note of a meeting with UNPROFOR on the 13th of August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't got that page, 336. Is it maybe 236?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, I'm sorry. That's what I think I said. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radojko, that's right. And in particular, you have a long note of something that you have recorded Mr. Odobasic as saying. Before we look at that, do you recall when you recorded this? In other words, how contemporaneous with Mr. Odobasic saying these words did you write them down?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did write this down while he was talking to the UNPROFOR representatives. We were at the meeting together. I recorded his arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we see that he said: "Bare existence is under threat, because it is impossible to obtain foodstuffs, the rights to work and education cannot be secured, nobody can guarantee security because of extremists and the psychosis of war. The situation is bearable, but nobody can say with certainty when it can become dangerous, afterwards it could be too late ... The authorities themselves are having problems with extremists, for example, when Serbian soldiers are wounded or killed. "To remain in Petrovac would be a catastrophe for us. "They also wish to exchange prisoners from Kamenica."

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talked about the situation as it was then, and he presented it fairly. The Muslim part of our delegation had separate talks with the foreign representatives. Well, probably in order for this to be, well, in a way, more appropriate. Husein Odobasic is actually saying what everybody was afraid of: Serbs and Muslims, if there are massive deaths, then everything will break loose and what had already started will go on, and that is to say general mayhem, killing, shooting, violence. You see, that's what people were afraid of. He was also aware of the fact that the authorities were powerless before this torrent. He knew it and other members of the delegation knew it. That is why a way out was sought. By the way, they actually want to have an exchange of the prisoners from Kamenica. I don't know who it was that spoke about this, perhaps it was the Muslims. There were some Muslim soldiers who had been taken prison and who were in Kamenica, so this had to do with military fugitives and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we also see the entry which follows, which says: "For the UN it is important that it is possible to meet the Muslims, representatives of their authorities and their military representative in normal conditions ..." Was that facilitated? If so, how? When? And by who?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made these notes for myself to convey this to the president, that is to say, what the representatives of UNPROFOR had said, that it was important for them to be able to have normal meetings with everyone. And -- well, I mean, without forcing anyone to do anything, bringing anyone to meetings by force or whatever. Well, they simply wanted to have this communication, for as long as the general atmosphere was civilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please get an idea of this Captain Odobasic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He wasn't a captain. He was just a prominent citizen, but an ordinary citizen. After the Muslim leaders who contributed the most to sowing this hatred between the different communities, they fled to Bihac and to other destinations with the help of leaders. These citizens remained at the mercy of this fire that they had set. So this Odobasic appeared and it was his community that delegated him to talk to the Crisis Staff and to the other representatives to see what kind of solution could be found for them. He was an entrepreneur, a small-scale entrepreneur. He actually had a little grocery store, so he used to sell fruit and vegetables, things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sorry to have called him "captain" but he was called "captain" on the documents I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says "Philippe La Vergne, Captain." This is a French captain, commander of that unit where we came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like you to look at page 244, the 17th of August of 1992, page 137 in translation. This relates to a meeting that day with the UNHCR. It mentions the military observers, French major, an English major, a Russian major, and there was an interpreter. And then you set out the position of those you were speaking to. Were there Muslim representatives at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. As a rule, they always went to these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And again, the note, was it contemporaneous?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recorded their positions in order to be able to transmit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure we've all read what it now says. What was your view of what these negotiators, these international foreign negotiators, were saying to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed their positions verbatim. I personally did not have any objections vis-a-vis these views, although I had indicated the problem involved and why people were coming. Maybe they had talked on their own; I cannot remember. But at any rate, often when people like that came they wanted to hear Muslims on their own. For example, if I were the only Serb on a particular delegation, sometimes I would stay somewhere else and they would talk to the Muslims only. That's the way it was in Licki Petrovac [as interpreted] and perhaps in some other places, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, so far as this diary is concerned, on the next page, 246, the 18th of August, 1992, we see a reference to five lambs. I don't think we need to worry about that. It's the next entry that I'd like to ask you about. It says: "Connection of one telephone Sefko or Husein Odobasic (resolved by a decision of the War Presidency)." Tell us about that and why that decision was made.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that -- well, when I read notes, I remember some things and I said that quite a few Serb numbers were disconnected as well because perhaps all of Petrovac did not have more than 1200 or 1500 numbers. At that time there were very few telephone lines, generally speaking, so quite a few Serbs were disconnected as well. Perhaps Muslims more speaking in terms of percentages, but what this is about is that these people, who were sort of prominent citizens, it was people from their own ethnic group who thought that they were prominent people. They wanted their telephones to be turned on so they could communicate with the rest of the world. These were people who by the very logic of things were considered to be people who would not spread any propaganda or react hysterically, so that is why this certain number of telephones was connected, and then it went up. This was just for the sake of communication, in order to be able to talk, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the witness could be given tab 37, please, which is P90, tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am perhaps a bit slow, Mr. Josse, but I'm still -- I'm reading the last answer. You say: "When I read the notes, I remember some things," and you said, "quite a few Serb numbers were disconnected as well because perhaps all of Petrovac did not have more than 1200 or 1500 numbers." Is my recollection well when disconnection, we saw earlier during your testimony, was 800 numbers of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Muslims for the most part. The restriction affected them to a higher degree, so in terms of percentages, that's the way it was. That was the impression I had from these talks. Your Honour, it is very hard for me to be very specific and accurate after all this time, and you have to understand that I had just arrived in that town at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm trying to understand, again the logic. You say: "Quite a few Serb numbers were disconnected as well because perhaps all of Petrovac did not have more than 1200 or 1500 numbers." What -- what's the logic that quite a few Serb numbers were disconnected as well because there were no more than 1200 to 1500 numbers? I mean, what's -- I have difficulties in following again the logic. You say "because," so there seems to be a causal relation -- at least, the one follows from the other, and I'm unable to follow it. Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. I understand that you do not realise the technical aspect involved. Well, this is what it's all about -- I didn't know it either at the time. This is what it's all about: I read these notes here, and I had forgotten that as well, so this jogged my memory. Petrovac, after being switched from the Bihac to the Banja Luka switchboard, telephone exchange, the entire municipality had only 12 lines, that is to say that only 12 telephone conversations could be taking place at one given point in time with Petrovac. And that is why the number of users was severely restricted. Because if everybody had remained connected, practically, those official lines that were indispensable for work purposes could never have had an opportunity to have their telephone conversations. The police, the military, the municipal authorities and the top levels of companies and institutions had access to these telephone lines. Once this was taken care of, then others could use the telephone lines as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not an explanation, but it's a new element in the testimony of this witness. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The document that I hope you now have in front of you, Mr. Radojko, is a report by something called the Bosanski Petrovac Expatriots' Club based in Zagreb. Prior to coming to The Hague, had you heard of this Expatriots' Club?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hadn't heard of that before. It was during my last testimony that I first heard of this, but it had become customary for everybody to set up these expatriots clubs wherever they had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to read this report?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is whether, in your view, it's a fair report on the events in Bosanski Petrovac from June 1992 until the departure of these expatriots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's -- counsel's certainly entitled to go into it, but that aspect of the -- it was -- I don't understand the nature of this question. That was asked and answered very clearly before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember, as a matter of fact, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It sounds like a foundational question, and that foundation was covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- well, Mr. Josse, it's not in my memory, but Mr. Tieger says that this has been asked and has been answered and it's a foundational question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've obviously asked the question very poorly. What I wanted the witness to comment upon was whether, in his view, this is a true recollection of events; whether it's accurate, whether the Court can rely upon it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness can answer it again, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly when it was, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the time the -- I mean -- you want me to find it in the transcript, Your Honour? I'll try. It was certainly when I brought the witness's attention to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must have missed it -- Well, the Bench remembers --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to hand out some copies of P1054. There's plenty here. The witness will not be familiar with this, the Chamber and my learned friend will be. It's a list of deputies attending Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, as we can see, it says the numbers on the right-hand side indicate the number of sessions from which the deputy was absent. I would like to ask you to look at number 54, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you read out the name in number 54 slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 54 is Dragan Milanovic, a deputy from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dragan Milanovic, not Milakovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see it's been put on the ELMO, Your Honour. I've got lots more copies here if anyone else need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was the deputy from Petrovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Petrovac have any other deputies?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet Hidic, until he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He, presumably, wasn't in the Assembly of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, he went to Bihac and then to Zagreb even before the Muslims started leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could you read the three sessions that it appears Mr. Milanovic was absent from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I do understand that this is needed in the common-law tradition, but if you would just have said that on that list we see Dragan Milanovic - because the K is only in English and not in B/C/S - being absent at the 17th, the 20th, and the 31st, then that would certainly go more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Clearly the Defence wants to establish that Mr. Milanovic wasn't at the 17th in particular. At the 20th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you say, we can read this here, could you confirm or not confirm if he was there or not, that takes approximately a third of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do appreciate that you are following what you're traditionally asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I've been taught to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And now we try to dissuade you against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, any need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, if I could ask you to turn once again to page 224 of your diary. I'm just going to bring you back to a couple of references Mr. Josse brought your attention to. And that was a reference to prevention of unauthorised occupation of abandoned property from -- a reference that appears in your diary on August 9th. Now, this is right around the time that the Crisis Staff was demanding and obtaining property abandonment or relinquishment certificates from Muslims, as reflected in the two certificates we saw, I believe yesterday, dated August 10th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible. I don't recall whether they tallied, but I do believe that they all did from this same period. This here has to do with the property of the people who already left. Many people left of their own will and on their own initiative. Whoever had enough money left far earlier. Some of them went to the neighbouring places, others went on a convoy that had gone somewhat earlier, and there were many empty houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd very much like that you answer the question Mr. Tieger puts to you. The only question put to you -- whether it was a necessary question, Mr. Tieger, is another matter, because the Chamber at least is aware that the 10th of August is close to the 9th. But of course I can imagine that you want to draw the attention of the witness to that and then put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I intended to. I didn't anticipate that -- I didn't attempt to elicit and didn't anticipate the lengthy answer that followed, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then perhaps you would stop the witness if he goes beyond what you asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I will do so, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'm not focussing on the property of those who left earlier; I'm focussing on the property of those leaving around that time, particularly those who were obliged to give up their property permanently to the Petrovac municipality. That property would have -- that was property that the Crisis Staff and the municipality intended to deal with and distribute on its own. Correct? That was property --

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to speculate about their intentions, but if you ask me whether I believe that those were their intentions, no, I don't. This has to do with property that had been abandoned earlier on. Those who signed the certificates remained in their houses until they left. So it wasn't their houses that were barged into, but rather the houses that were abandoned, that didn't have their owners around anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, as a general matter with respect to both the property it -- that was the subject of the certificates we saw yesterday, that is property left specifically and expressly to the municipality, and with respect to any other property that might have been abandoned, the Crisis Staff wanted to be in a position to make decisions about who would occupy that property. Which of the incoming refugees, for example, would be able to occupy it. Whether or not some property should be given to families of soldiers, and so on. That was the responsibility that the Crisis Staff wanted to undertake. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect, yes; for the accommodation of refugees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it was inconsistent with that and a problem for the Crisis Staff if others arbitrarily occupied those premises. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was unacceptable because some of the local residents started occupying abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next to page 220 -- 236, excuse me, of your translation; page 133 of the English translation. That's the diary entry of August 13th to which Mr. Josse directed your attention; the meeting with the French captain, Odobasic, Druzic, and so on. Now, Mr. Josse pointed out the reference at the bottom of that entry and that you commented on that the UN wanted to meet Muslims in the absence of representatives from -- in the absence of Serbian representatives. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand. UNPROFOR -- or rather, UNPROFOR representatives said that they wanted to meet with everyone, not only with the Muslims or someone who would gather information from the Serb side, but rather with the actual representatives of the army, with the people who have the authority to make decisions rather than meeting up with only Muslims or with someone who did not have any decision-making authority, if I've made myself clear enough. They wanted to see people who can take decisions, if I remember well, and I do believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the entry in your diary of the importance of the UN to meet Muslims and the representatives of their authorities and military authorities in normal conditions did not reflect any concern on their part that the information they were getting from Muslims might not be as reliable as it would be if they met with Muslims in the absence of representatives of the Serbian authorities. That would make some sense, though, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it a fact, Mr. Radojko, that -- isn't it a fact that some of the information indeed that UNPROFOR was getting from Serbian representatives was, shall we say, a little slanted and one-sided and didn't represent the full picture of what was happening to Muslims in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Petrovac is concerned, they had first-hand information from the people there. They even talked to them separately, on their own. I don't know why only one side should be present. I didn't provide them with any information. The only party who could provide them with one-sided, inaccurate information was me, but even if -- had I provided them with such information, they spoke with the Muslims on their own on several occasions. It says here they should meet with the Muslims, then with the representatives of the authorities and a military representative. Now why? Because they already knew that the Muslims were not represented by those in the authorities, that they had already left the municipality many, many months earlier; in the month of May or even earlier. This meant that they wanted to meet with the representatives -- the official representatives of the Serb authorities and a military representative, that's to say a representative of the Serbian army, which means that they wanted to relay their position to these people directly and not through me as a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just focussing on the notes in your diary, which are meetings that you attended, which are obviously not meetings at which Muslims only were present. So in that respect if I can ask you to turn to another diary entry to which Mr. Josse directed your attention, that's page 244 of your diary, August 17th. Now, in fairness to you I'll -- I recall that you indicated that your recollection was that most of the time Muslims were present, but to be quite accurate, your diary, of course, does not reflect the presence of any Muslim at this particular meeting. So to the extent we're depending on the diary rather than your recollection of general events, it would seem to indicate that this was a meeting between you and international representatives. I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that be turned into a question, if it be a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is indeed a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I just want to know if you have any specific recollection of who was there, sir, or, as you were indicating to the Court, it was just your general recollection that Muslim representatives were usually present at such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't really remember a meeting which they did not attend. I have to admit I don't recall where this meeting was held, whether it was in Petrovac, Knin, Licko Petrovo Selo. If it was in Licko Petrovo Selo, then I know for a fact that Muslim representatives were there and I only sat out for part of the meeting because they asked me to leave the room because they wanted to finish the meeting outside my presence. And I'm talking about this meeting on the 17th of August. It's possible that I did not make note of their presence because I was part of the delegation. Wherever the delegation was, I was, and vice versa. I can't remember, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just focus on the first part of this note: "They will not take part in re-settlement, that is unacceptable in war, economic reasons, unemployment is the same for the Serbs and that is not the reason for re-settlement." "They will not take part in re-settlement," that's a reference to the international community refusing to take part?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Odobasic presented the reasons, and their answer was a firm one, was this one. There were still some prospects for them to actually organise to help with the convoy at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. It's not pleasant to have to interrupt you but you need to listen to my question and just answer it, please. All right. And -- so the answer is: "Yes, they --" the reference "they will not take part" is a reference to the international community. And the reason given the international community, as reflected in your minutes, and the reason rejected by the international community, was economic reasons, unemployment. Correct? That's what these representatives of the international community were told, and that's the reason they rejected.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They rejected this for safety reasons as well. You have to know that it's quite difficult to make note of everything as people speak. They rejected this for security reasons as well. It's not -- that's not written here, but the only reasons not mentioned -- or rather, not reflected here are the security reasons, and the security also referring to the Serbs who were staying behind. You see, it says here they want -- or rather, the local authorities to protect them and that -- they want for the aid to be equally distributed. So the gist of it is there. They do know that there are security reasons at issue here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's just focus on the economic reasons. The international representatives understood from their discussion with you - whoever else was present - that you were saying that economic reasons that applied equally to Serbs as Muslims was prompting the desire by Muslims to leave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Economic reasons, too. I have to explain to you why they were in an economically less favourable position. With the start of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, please, I don't want to hear an explanation of that. I want to know -- I've asked you what they were told on this occasion, you've explained. And they were led to believe -- they rejected that, but it's clear that you didn't explain to them in any way that the unemployment situation for Muslims was dramatically worse by virtue of the actions of the Crisis Staff. Correct? That Muslims were being discharged. That part wasn't explained to the representatives of the international community, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct. As far as I remember, the situation was described to them in great detail. As I said, this was crucial, not only for the Muslims but also for the Serbs because the overwhelming majority of them were unemployed, but you didn't allow me to give you the explanation of it. But the two ethnic groups were not in the same economic position --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And despite your -- what must have been a fairly dramatic explanation of the situation in which Muslims were being discharged from their jobs, these international representatives failed to grasp that, commenting that unemployment was the same for Serbs. So they missed that whole point of your explanation, is what you're saying. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally -- well, two more things. One with respect to the issue of the telephones the Judge -- that you spoke with His Honour about. I had one question about that as well. As you've indicated earlier, Petrovac was an overwhelming Serb municipality. So I'd like to know how it is that if Petrovac had only 1200 to 1500 phone lines, that Muslims had 800 of them at the time all Muslims -- all 800 Muslims were -- had their telephone service cut?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, you're now pinning me down on one word, and I was giving you my opinion. First of all, I hadn't been in Petrovac for quite a long time and I wasn't dealing with those problems. I believe -- and at the end of the day it's easy to verify how many telephone lines Petrovac had. Whether it was 1.000, or 1.500, I don't know, but I can tell you, and I said clearly, that among the 800 people whose lines were disconnected, there were also Serbs, although it was mostly Muslims who had their telephone lines disconnected. But this wasn't central to what I was doing at the time. I was listening to information being presented and this was something that was given by the way, and now you're trying to put words into my mouth. At the end of the day the Muslim intelligence service seized this documentation and gave it over to you has all the information. You have telephone directories from before the war and one can easily double-check how many there were, and you're trying to establish what the number was through me by implying that I'm not telling the truth. I was telling you things from memory, and you keep giving me documents which contain the exact precise information. Do you recall facts from 15 years back? I was expelled twice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, please listen carefully to the questions put to you by Mr. Tieger and answer them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, having disconnected all Muslim numbers, as the diary reference of June 13th that we looked at yesterday indicates, it would have been necessary, would it not, to at least connect the telephone of one or maybe two Muslims in order to assure their attendance at meetings with UNPROFOR designed for the purpose of moving them out of the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not because of that. Not all these lines were disconnected -- I mean of all the Muslims. For instance, the head of the post office was a Muslim and I don't believe his telephone line was disconnected. But to tell you the truth, I don't know. But it wasn't just with UNPROFOR that people communicated. I don't think we could even establish a direct line with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The connection that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it short. We're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was a serious suggestion that was made to the witness; he's entitled to deal with it. If my learned friend is going to make allegations like that, the witness is entitled to deal with it fully. It's an extremely loaded question and got a long response, unsurprisingly, in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll ask three brief questions in that regard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Husein Odobasic the Odobasic who attended the meetings reflected earlier in your diary?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the decision by the connection of one telephone, either to Sefko or Husein Odobasic required a decision by the War Presidency, right, as reflected in your diary on 18 August 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last question? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is: This is something I thought had been done and intended to do yesterday. If I could distribute this to the witness and the Court. This is -- the Court will recall tab 22, the list of 29 persons taken to Kozila on July 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you can just look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this needs a number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to be more difficult than I have to be. Where is the original? Is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there any B/C/S version of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's primarily a list of names, but I appreciate the -- no, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's quite a lot of common --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. Could I have a moment to look at the original before any questions are asked? I see there's a lot of information at the back of the original, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which seems not to be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd also like to inquire what this document is before it's put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may -- Mr. Tieger, may I take it that the English version, the last, I would say, six pages, starting ERN number last three digits 290 could be taken off because there seems not to be any translation of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We take off the last three pages -- five pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should go to English translation 353 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And list -- person listed at number 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, now we are back with the list only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Are we going to get the provenance of it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was seized from Bosanski Petrovac, along with all the -- basically all the other documents we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'll listen to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this particular document came from the Petrovac SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radojko, my quick look at this indicates -- seems to indicate the name of about nine or ten of the same people who appear at the list in tab 22 that you -- that was introduced into evidence, or that you had a chance to look at the other day. That's at tab 22 of the materials that we've been looking at, if you want to look at that again. And if I can be of assistance, you might see, for example, the name of Husein Kartal, Fadil Kartal, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd just like to know two things: Number one, if you can confirm that the overlap of people from both lists; and number two, if both lists contain, to the best of your knowledge, the names of only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JOVO RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by their names, they are indeed all Muslims. But at first glance, I don't seem to know any of them. But judging by their names, they are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness go out, I've got a point I wish to raise about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got one problem, Mr. Josse: How much time would we still need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I may need a fair amount of time. Perhaps I could address the Chamber about it and voice my concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. At the same time, we are close to a break and if you would need considerable time, we would have to break anyhow. Would this result in any further examination, whether re-examination, cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will almost certainly apply to re-examine the witness further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then we can't finish at this moment. You'll have an opportunity to address the Chamber after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand the importance of criminal procedure, especially in a court of law. At the same time, the Court -- our core business is to hear evidence and not to see what kind of procedural issues -- of course I do not know what you will bring us, Mr. Josse, but I noticed that especially the last couple of days we had more procedural incidents than -- and I'm not saying you're to be blamed for it, I'm looking to Mr. Tieger as well, but I'm just expressing my concern about it. We'll have a break. We'll re-start at 25 minutes past 4.00, and the witness should be stand-by at that moment to re-enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask for a little bit more time? I want to go in to briefly see the next witness to see if he's all right, and I would like to look at this document closely. It may be that a half an hour break would help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll re-start at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you asked not only for time but even considerable time. I said something about procedural issues. I want to avoid what we're at risk to do yesterday, to re-visit Browne v. Dunn again on the Rule 90(H)(ii), go into the ways it is applied everywhere. I think it was not of major importance, but let's try to keep our procedural issues really to the point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the last document that concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The time has been valuable. Mr. Tieger very helpfully has informed me - without my asking him, it's fair to say - that he accepts that he should have pointed out that this document clearly does not arise from my re-examination and, therefore, needless to say, I am entitled to re-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the first remarks I made to my colleagues when we left this courtroom. Yes, he -- what he was not allowed to do yesterday, he thought he will find the time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I, as I say, I immediately told Mr. Josse, and I apologise to the Court. I had intended to bring that to the attention -- bring my understanding to the attention of the Court and ask their permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am somewhat perturbed by this document, but before I re-examine on it, perhaps I could submit that it shouldn't be admitted into evidence, that the witness's response to the questions he was asked don't provide sufficient foundation for its admission into evidence. And if the Court was so to rule at this stage, then I wouldn't need to ask any further questions of the witness. If the Court's against me on that, then I would like to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, why should we read this list in order to know that when Mujaga Didovic was taken into custody that it was noted that she threatened Serbs as a child? Or what are we supposed to learn from this which adds to what we know already?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, my examination of that indicates that approximately ten of the people on this list appear on the name of the list provided before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's useful in that respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't the list about, from what I see, stopping cars and perhaps arresting people. I take it that everyone who was in custody was arrested prior to being in custody. I would not expect, under those circumstances, Muslims knocking at the door of a detention facility and saying: Please let me in. So for that purpose, unless, Mr. Josse, you would disagree, that if someone would be detained, that it's fair to accept that he was arrested before kept in detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's -- for that purpose, therefore, we hardly need it, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's not to show that they were arrested but just the ostensible bases for those arrests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and now, could this witness, do you think, tell us anything about -- of course we see on this list that one person taken into custody was also known as Pike, or -- well, of course there are some matters, I take it, that you -- one was a criminal and a nationalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, if I can explain quickly, maybe it will help resolve it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this is a document that might have more -- understandably, come in as a contextual document or in a dossier or something of that nature. It just occurred to me that because this witness was here, Mr. Josse would want to see this document. And I also think from the witness's answer he doesn't know these individual people, which would have made it even more appropriate as a contextual document. So in that context, I have no problem. Just as an abundance of caution I thought I would present it here so if the witness did know any of those people he could comment on them, if Mr. Josse so chose. And that was my only rationale for doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This witness told us that he doesn't know these people. Of course, we could ask him to read all the names once again. Mr. Josse, would it be appropriate, would it be a solution, to further discuss the admission of this document as a -- not perhaps at this very moment, but to, at a later stage, consider whether this could be admitted as a contextual document. At the same time I'm aware, Mr. Tieger, that we're now hearing the Defence case rather than the Prosecution case. That might need some further thought as well as to what extent new contextual exhibits should be admitted during the presentation of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm bound to say that I agree with Mr. Tieger to this extent: If it's going to be admitted, it should be admitted having been put to the witness, allowing the Defence to deal with it in re--examination. So I submit that it should not be admitted as a contextual document. If it's going to be admitted, it should be admitted in the way that Mr. Tieger's presented it, and as I've made quite clear, I oppose that in any event for the reasons I've already set out. I hope my position is plain on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say: If it were to be admitted, it should be admitted in the way Mr. Tieger proposed, but even then you would strongly oppose against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. And I ask for a ruling now for the reasons I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber gives a ruling. The Chamber does not admit this document at this moment through this witness. If ever a request would be on our table to admit it as a contextual document, the Chamber is aware that it would cause a lot of serious legal questions, we'll then consider them, but it might that it never happens and then we don't have to answer all these serious legal -- give an answer to all these serious legal issues. That's the ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then, when the witness comes back into court, I'm going to say I have no further questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we gave the document a number already. That means that number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1108 would be available, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As Your Honour's aware, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radojko, Mr. Josse has no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since the Bench has no question, Mr. Tieger, I take it that -- let me just see -- yes, I should ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm amazed but very pleased you turned to me, Your Honour, but I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see -- okay. Mr. Radojko, since the Bench has no further questions to you either, this means that this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the, well, very far way to The Hague and to testify to answer questions put to you, both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as far as exhibits are concerned -- there are not many new exhibits. Most of the exhibits in the binders were exhibits that were already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, for this particular witness I can say with a fair degree of confidence that the only document I'm going to oppose the admission of is - I'm just checking the number - P1014, I think it was -- excuse me whilst I try and get my list -- which was the document from the humanitarian organisation -- the Reuters --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm guessing 1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 1104, the Reuters document. I'm in the Court's hands as to when the Court wishes to hear the argument on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- let me see. How much time would it take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes. Please take your two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence submit that this is exactly the sort of document that the Court should not admit into evidence. It is a hearsay account from a reporting organisation. The witness did not accept the small part that was put to him. My learned friend only chose to put a small part to him; he didn't accept its accuracy. It's of no probative value, in our submission, and if it is of any probative value at all, its prejudicial value so outweighs any probative value as to mean the Court should have no hesitation in refusing its submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I may have mis-cited it. I know it was in the 1100 series or so, but I don't know if that's the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1100 series sounds like cars, Mr. Tieger, but we talk exhibits. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this argument is unfounded because it's misdirected in large measure. I think counsel's concern is about the admission of newspaper accounts that purport by themselves to prove that events happened. At a minimum, this document is about the kind of information available to the authorities, the kind of information that was disseminated. There was considerable discussion during the course of his -- during the course of his testimony about propaganda and the various uses and impacts of information disseminated, as he said, by either side. In this particular case, by Bosnian Serb authorities. This document goes directly to that, both to what information was available to the Bosnian Serbs from international organisations and what information was being disseminated to international organisations from the Bosnian Serb authorities. And at a minimum, as evidence of notice and about contemporaneous events, that is, UNPROFOR or international -- the declarations of international organisations, it's clearly probative and clearly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I suggest the following to the parties: In the course -- during the testimony of Mr. Radojko -- testimony of Mr. Radojko, often numbers were assigned, were withdrawn at a later stage. Sometimes numbers given to exhibits that were already in evidence. The registrar is invited to prepare an updated list of all the documents that were introduced through Mr. Radojko. We'll have that on the table at our next session, our next hearing. We'll then also give our ruling on the admission of 1104, the Reuters report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready to be called by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, he's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's my first observation. Frankly, the Defence logistical position, leave aside the witness's situation, is not exactly what I might have hoped. I had thought that I had arranged to have copied all the sessions of the Republika Srpska government in 1992. That has not happened. A number of those sessions are relevant. We thought we would produce a comprehensive bundle which, frankly, might be useful later on. Your Honour, let me see how far I can go and get without that material. Could I make this inquiry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
