utterances.text: -- I don't know whether there exists a comprehensive set of government sessions. Mr. Margetts, who's been very helpful and is dealing with this witness, tells me that he has only selective sessions in the bundle that he's prepared for the witness, which I can well understand. I wonder whether the Prosecution have one or more bundles of the full run. If they don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- again I can well understand. There's no reason why they should. I'm not trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I know that some of these huge binder series in evidence, I never know which type of document to find in which -- under which number. But -- let me just have a look. For example, I know that we have the P64, binders 1 to 28, et cetera. If we find them somewhere in there -- I'm a bit concerned about, again, cutting down a whole wood, and at least the Bench has some access to electronic versions of documents that are already in evidence. I take it that the same is true for the Prosecution. Prosecution could put that on the screen. So therefore, I wonder whether we have to produce another series of binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the good news is I've got a complete set, so my set could go on the screen, if need be. My team produced one set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we now refrain from driving the copying machines to madness and rather see if we can cope with what we have at this very moment. Mr. Margetts --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, the Defence machine is in the asylum already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the asylum already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would be able to locate a version suitable for us electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we could then put that on the screen. And may I ask you, Mr. Margetts, in what -- under what exhibit number would we find most? Because I've got quite a lot on my computer. I'm not certain that I have the complete series, but where would I have to look mainly? Would it be in P529 or P64 or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I would expect P64A, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P64A, there I've got 28 binders and I have -- I have it all up to binder 12, I'm afraid, that we've come that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It is the fact that we have an electronic file with all of the translations in that file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And we could put that on disk and provide it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- to the Court. Not the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is mainly to get it in the right place in our computer so we can -- Mr. Josse, I suggest that we just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you are invited to start and we can see how far we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Lakic. Mr. Josse, would you prefer that I put a few initial questions to the witness or would you rather start and see whether at any given moment there would be a need to put some questions to the witness about today's events?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me start, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your name is Nedeljko Lakic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were born in Trebinje and went to school there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You then got a law degree in Sarajevo and --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- began working in the Bosnian MUP?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You worked for a short time in the Ministry of Defence and --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- then you were employed with the professional services of the government of Bosnia; a civil servant, in effect?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1979, you were appointed as an under-secretary to the cabinet of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were a member of the Communist Party until 1990?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, you worked in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, and your job was secretary to the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was a position you held from 1983 until the outbreak of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the outbreak of the war, you went to live in Pale and shortly thereafter - and we'll go into the details later - you became secretary to the cabinet or government of the Republika Srpska, a position you held till 1998?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Secretary of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When the government of the Republika Srpska moved to Banja Luka, you took a job there as a government inspector. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And eventually you received employment with the BiH government, for whom you presently work?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon: The Presidency of the B & H.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, thank you very much for clarifying that. And you basically work now in a part-time capacity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I've retired two years ago, and then they gave me a contract, a work contract as a free-lancer. I am paid for the amount of time I spend working. As for the rest of my income, it is from my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to first, in terms of my substantive questions, ask you about the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. What was the purpose of that council, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: The Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order was a working body, basically a working body, which prepared material for meetings of the Presidency, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: And basically it could not pass any independent decisions; it just prepared material for sessions of the Presidency. May I? These materials were prepared on the basis of material that were submitted by ministries whose members were on the council itself. The council was constituted on an ethnic basis. It consisted of representatives of all three constituent peoples. So that is as regards ethnicity. As regards substance, it consisted of representatives of the government, the Assembly, and the Ministry of the Interior. When necessary, other representatives of different bodies could attend government sessions if their material was on the agenda. That would be it, as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, were any ethnic tensions demonstrated by anything that went on in the council?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These ethnic tensions could be felt. There was a hint of such tensions in immediate contacts that took place, that is to say, among citizens of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was true to a lesser degree in relations among different organs of the institutions of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to give a normal example as far as citizens are concerned. For example, if people were talking in a mono-ethnic setting, if I can put it that way, if somebody who was of a different ethnic background would come in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me help you a little bit, Mr. Lakic. If you could be a bit more specific. I particularly would like you to tell the Trial Chamber about the way ethnic tensions reared their head in any of the activities of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order prior to 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: In 1990 elections were held. Nationalist parties won that election. I think that the tensions, the ethnic tensions, started from then on, that is to say, after the victory of the nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite the Chamber to ask the witness to step outside and then for the Chamber to go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lakic, could you, for one second, follow Madam Usher, leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour, we're emptying the gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would private session do, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's not possible, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in this courtroom it doesn't -- it doesn't resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. For the parties to know, I -- during the break I instructed the registry to strike one question put by me and one answer given by the witness from the public record. Our information is that there's no reason at this moment not to continue, so therefore, Madam Usher, I'd like you to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Lakic. Mr. Lakic, the Chamber understands that it's a new environment for you and that you might not immediately have felt at ease. We took an additional break for some time. Whenever you'd feel that you have difficulties in either understanding the questions or if you feel at unease, please ask whatever you'd like to ask to me in those circumstances, or request -- if you'd say: I'd rather now have an additional break of a quarter of an hour, please ask me. So we will go slowly on. And before the break I put one question to you and you've answered that question. That specific question, you may remember what question it -- I may point at, it's stricken from the record, so that's not public anymore. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. And the answer was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take that the answer is correct, but the whole question, inclusive answer, has been stricken from the record. So that's not public at this moment. Mr. Josse -- Mr. Josse will now continue to examine you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When we broke off, Mr. Lakic, I was asking you about how really in 1991 ethnic tensions manifested themselves in the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: This was 15 years ago; that's why I cannot be specific in my answers. It's been a long time ago. I did not expect there to be any questions pertaining to council meetings. I believe it was at the 12th Session of the council -- or rather, that it was the 12th Session of the council which proved to be very important for the ethnic relationship in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The meeting was convened by Biljana Plavsic, who was a member of the Presidency and on the council --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because -- let me help you to this degree: My question was specifically general. I'm sure the Chamber understands it's a long time ago. Perhaps if we have a look at a document, that might assist you in relation to a particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm about to distribute a bundle which, I should say, the Prosecution had not had till a few minutes ago. It contains documents primarily, but not exclusively, that have previously been exhibited. There is a slight problem with tab 1 in a number of these editions, but not in the witness's, and I've explained to my learned friends. The witness's tab 1 is correct, deliberately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So that's for the witness and there are other bundles for the Court and interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first document is already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. It's P64A, and it's tab 1 that I'm going to -- part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic -- yes, Madam Usher, could you take care that the papers are not touching the microphone, because that's what causes the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. As I was saying, it's part of P64A --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Binder and tab numbers are not available?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Margetts has been very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's been very helpful on some other documents. I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll attempt to find the footnote number that corresponds to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, mainly binder and tab numbers, that's how they appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I think there may be some confusion with the Treanor exhibits. P65 had binder and tab numbers. P64A referred to the footnotes to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'm a bit lost, quite lost. Let's proceed. Let's see how far we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lakic, firstly, this is the 13th Session of the council that you are looking at. It took place in Sarajevo on the 9th of March, 1992. Is this the meeting you were beginning to tell the Chamber about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the session of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. This particular session was exceptionally significant, in my opinion, because at this meeting the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was examined. The main conclusion at -- of the council was that the political situation was a drastic one and that a civil war might break out. In order to avert this, the council decided that all -- any and all measures be taken in that preventing the outbreak of a conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This primarily had to do with the reorganisation of the army because the SDA - Alija Izetbegovic's party, that is - asked that all Muslim members, now called Bosniaks, withdraw, and almost all of them did withdraw. The council asked that the army be reorganised in such a way that the new organisation reflected the ethnic make-up of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second conclusion was that, to the same end, the Ministry of the Interior be reorganised, that its human resources be improved and its work enhanced. There were also requests that the reserve police force and the TO be activated. These two were part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the army. The third conclusion was that justice administration bodies, that's to say SUP, prosecutor's office and judiciary, improve the efficiency of their work and prevent any conflicts in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A more general conclusion followed from this, mainly that all state bodies of Bosnia-Herzegovina be active participants in this process. I believe that I have given you a resume of the council's position and -- a summary. And this particular document was delivered to all the state bodies in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The council could not make decisions on matters. It could only give recommendations to the state bodies, and every conclusion taken by the council is then further discussed by the government. Now, as to the reason why the presiding of the council -- the presiding person of the council convened this particular meeting which took place on the 12th of March, there were the 1990 elections preceding this which brought on tensions, as I've already said. It was, in particular, the events on the either the 28th or the 29th of February and on the 1st of March when Muslims and Croats took part in a -- in a referendum and decided at the referendum that the independence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina be declared. In this way the constitution was violated as well as the equality of the constituent -- of one constituent peoples, and namely Serbs. The constitution cannot be amended and a referendum cannot be called -- or rather, its results cannot be accepted unless there is a two-third majority in favour. As far as I remember, in 1990, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs constituted about 35 per cent of the population, and none of them participated in the referendum. In the aftermath of the referendum, there was general chaos in Sarajevo as well as in other parts of Bosnia, although I can speak for Sarajevo because that's where I live. In the areas where the Serbs constituted a majority, they erected roadblocks, and Muslims did the same in the areas where they were in a majority. In this period of time, a very grave matter occurred for Christians, and that was that Muslims murdered a member -- a guest at the wedding. And of course you have to understand that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, perhaps I can explain to you that quite a lot of things you've told us have been the subject of testimony of other witnesses as well. For example, the wedding you just mentioned that one of the guests was murdered; we've heard that several times. I therefore suggest to you that you carefully listen to what specifically Mr. Josse wants to know from you, because this Chamber has heard evidence already considerably, and we would like to hear what you could add, and Mr. Josse will put the questions to you in such a way because he knows what has been the testimonies until now, so that your information is added to what we already know. Mr. Josse, would you please keep this as well in mind if you put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm in a position to provide the details in relation to the first exhibit, which is the minutes of the 13th Session of the Council of the Protection for Constitutional Order. That is P64A, binder 4, footnote 46. And whilst I'm on my feet, Mr. Josse may proceed to tab 2, he may not, but if he could take a note of this, that's P64A, binder 25, footnote 718, 718.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Our exhibits are organised in a different way on the computer, so it finally does not assist me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And ours aren't organised at all, as is quite apparent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, what I'd like you to do is have a look at item 1, the agenda, the meeting on the 13th Session. And it says that: "All members of the Council in attendance participated in the discussion. They found the political/security situation in SR Bosnia-Herzegovina critical and that large-scale conflicts and civil war may be expected if appropriate measures are not taken immediately. "It was agreed to make the following proposals: "1) Relevant government authorities and institutions must be able to guarantee that rule of law shall prevail in the country, and that constitutionality and legality are observed. In this respect, the presence of paramilitary among all the three peoples in the Republic should be considered a priority issue." I want to ask you about that last sentence, please. When this meeting was taking place in March of 1992, what was your understanding of the state of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, while reading, you -- the French interpreters get a backlog, and so would you please read a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, what was your understanding at the time of this meeting of the state of paramilitaries among the three ethnic communities of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am of the same opinion -- or rather, I formulated these positions that the council eventually adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what paramilitaries were you aware of so far as Serbs were concerned?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I think it had to do with the White Eagles. At this stage I cannot recall anyone else, but I know that on the Muslim side the SDA -- a year earlier two paramilitary structures were set up which Alija Izetbegovic recognised before his passing away at an SDA Assembly session. As for the Croats, I wouldn't be able to tell you which these were. However, as far as I know, the regular army of the Republic of Croatia crossed over into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Sijekovac, where a massacre was committed against Serbs. I wanted to use this as an illustration of the chaos which prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is one other part of this document I would like to ask you about. Could you look at number 5, please. We see it says --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under item 5 it is stated -- or rather, since it was stated that the national parties might have caused the situation, it was concluded that the army and the law enforcement agencies would be more efficient if the operation of these agencies was separated from the political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At this point in time, were you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that you left the Communist Party in 1990. Thereafter, did you ever join another political party?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was that and which party?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: In late 1993, into the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why did you join that party at that stage?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Because I thought that the person who does not belong to the Serb Democratic Party cannot hold any position anywhere in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why didn't you join that party in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Because I did not support the structuring of the state along ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In -- at about this time, were you secure in your job?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, that's my fault. In March 1992, just before the outbreak of the war, was your position within the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina secure?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Apologies: In the Presidency, within the Presidency. The Serbian Democratic Party practically removed me from the post of the secretary within the Presidency, and nobody offered me any other jobs. I believe that there was a decision by the Presidency on my removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at that, if we may, please. Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regret, this document isn't translated. This isn't a great deal of it we're going to need to look at, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're looking, aren't you, Mr. Lakic, at a -- the minutes from the 78th Session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 25th of April -- I beg your pardon, on the 24th of April, 1992, and I should have said this is the 77th Session. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything about any Presidency session. This particular session you mentioned was held on the 22nd of April and on the 23rd of April -- or rather, it was held on the 24th of April, and on the 25th of April I had already gone to Pale because that's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we're at cross-purposes. Turn the page, please, to item number 2.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see that under number 1 there's your name. Can you see your name there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you read out what it says after your name, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: "On the proposal of the Commission for Organisation and Personnel Matters of the RBiH Presidency, the Presidency took the following decision: Nedeljko Lakic is to be relieved from the duty of the republican advisor in the Presidency performing the duties of the secretary of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you understand - and in fairness to you, you've half explained this already - the reason that you were being removed from your job?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Because the Serb Democratic Party decided that I should be removed from the post and that another person - I believe his name is Radovan Leskovic [as interpreted] - should be appointed to that post. This took place before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's Radovan Neskovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I believe so. Radomir - I apologise - yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that you've not seen these minutes before and you were obviously not at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I could not; I was working at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that tab have a number, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 3, Your Honour, would be D146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, we've jumped ahead of the chronology a little bit, Mr. Lakic, so that you could deal with that. Why did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I explained this long ago: Ten years ago I built a family house at Pale that I used as a weekend cottage --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. You don't mean ten years ago from now, 2006; you mean ten years ago from 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I have been living in this house to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to tell the Trial Chamber, Mr. Lakic, about your reasons for leaving Sarajevo. You've explained that you had a home in Pale. It was a weekend-type home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It covers an area of 120 square metres. You call it as you like. I like to be physically active, and in spring-time and in summer-time I used to work tending my garden around the house. And in winter-time I went over there to ski. I have a wife and two sons, and we all ski. That's far closer to Mount Jahorina than Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. And -- perhaps I can be permitted to leave -- to lead. You left in April of 1992. Sarajevo, that is.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, or on the 4th -- well, either on the 3rd or on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was the reason that you left Sarajevo? The Chamber understands you had somewhere else to go, but why was it that you left Sarajevo, in effect, for good?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: The first reason was -- or rather, the main reason for my going there was of course to use it as a weekend cottage. The second reason was that a friend of mine, a Muslim, suggested that I should go over there, out of harm's way, because he was at Pale and he knew what the situation was. My son wore a red five-pointed star on a hat and they all called him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear what they called him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my friend told me that we should perhaps go to Pale just to lie low for a while. The other reason was that I was spending my time at Pale over the weekend and I wanted to go back because I was supposed to be on duty and this was Sunday afternoon. I boarded a bus that came from either Uzice or Kraljevo. I asked the driver whether the bus was headed for Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you're telling us a lot of details. What Mr. Josse, as far as I understood him, specifically wanted to know is not whether you went by bus or by car, but mainly why you left. I think you gave a clue to that answer when you said: "The second reason, that a friend of mine, a Muslim, suggested that I should go over there, out of harm's way." Mr. Josse, is that the portion you'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do hope I can be permitted to lead on this a little bit because we also think there may be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's right that your younger son, who was 17 at that point in time, was a big fan of Red Star football club?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And he was being abused because of that, ethnically abused?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They objected to that and he was a supporter, he was following his team in their footsteps, except for Tokyo, he didn't go over there, but he was just a sports fan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what -- was there anything that happened to your older son that was of importance?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He worked in the MUP, and this was at the time when the MUP had already split into two. He went back home to pick up his belongings - a suit, and some other items - when he got caught by the Green Berets, who locked him up and beat him up. They accused him of having fired from the rooftop of his house at the Green Berets. The Muslim who occupied the apartment upstairs came up and said: I assert to you that nobody fired any shots from the roof of my house today. I don't know how it came that the chief of the police station in charge of the neighbourhood where I lived got to know about this, and he got in touch with the Green Berets and asked them to bring my son over to them. One of those who was present when my elderly son was mistreated was called by the police commander and who said: Bring Nebojsa over to me. You should not lay your finger on him. And the other one did that immediately. In fact, later on it was suggested that fingertips be -- fingerprints be taken of him to establish whether indeed shots were fired. The police commander said: Nebojsa, I know that you were not responsible for this, but then perhaps you should leave the area and go over to this other area where the other police force was in charge. This was at the time when the police force was already divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened to your apartment in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: This was at Kozusko Brdo. This was an apartment belonging to the Presidency. It was locked up for a while; it was even sealed. Later on, when there was probably shortage of accommodation, they unsealed the apartment and put up refugees in there. I don't know where they hailed from. When I managed to get hold of the apartment - I went to great lengths to do that; thanks to international assistance, I did - but the apartment was completely destroyed. Since there -- I had some property in Trebinje as well, I exchanged properties with a physician from Trebinje and got an apartment in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So in the beginning of April of 1992, was it, that you and your younger son and wife moved to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you arrived in Pale, what did you live on?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I went to the Red Cross. [In English] Sorry. [Interpretation] I went to the Red Cross, but since I thought that I would be coming back, I did not really get ready and the apartment was practically empty. I had to help my family survive. I went to the Red Cross, and through the Red Cross I received aid in food and other provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about work? How did you set about finding a job?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Since I saw that it was not easy to get food from the Red Cross, I heard that some high officials had come to Pale as well, and I looked them up, and I first found Nikola Koljevic, the late Nikola Koljevic. Now, why did I look him up first? I worked with him in the Presidency, I knew him well, really well. Now, I can't remember who actually made this suggestion -- well, they knew what my career had been. They first suggested that I go to work in a magistrate's court, to organise the work of that court. I worked there for about a month -- well, about a month, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened in that month or after that month, in terms of a job?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I went to work every day, and I helped. There were two women judges, and I helped them organise the work of the misdemeanours court. I went to the Red Cross regularly and I brought food in order to feed my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how was it -- in what circumstances did you come to leave that job and become government secretary?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I had a lot of people I knew in Pale, people who had gone out to Pale. One day Trifo Komad came and he said that I was being asked to work for the government and that I should report to Branko Djeric, the Prime Minister. I should note that before that I had never seen Mr. Djeric directly, I had only known of him through the media. The situation I found there was one of an initial stage of organisation and work, so I joined in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we can help put this into some form of time-frame by having a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this be put on the ELMO. Your Honour, this is a session of the National Security Council in the government of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated 27th of April 1992, the 5th Session, as it's known, and it has been exhibited a number of times in this case. I can give various numbers, if I need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give the simplest number, that's easiest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 583, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 583, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's the second page that we're going to need to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can see on the second page, can't we, Mr. Lakic, it says: "Appointment and dismissal: Nenad Jovanovic is dismissed from the post of government secretary and Nedeljko Lakic, a graduate lawyer, appointed to it."

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this is --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: The reason was that the gentleman we see here, Nenad Jovanovic, also with a degree in law, he came to work in Pale and in this council before me. He got sick, and after that he had a very serious operation, eye operation. Perhaps it even ended tragically. So it was health reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, could I have those documents back.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A short while ago you told the Chamber that at about this time, certainly March of 1992, the SDS were trying to remove you from your job within the BiH government. Why was it --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: No, not the BH government, the Presidency of the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're quite right to correct me. Either way, the -- a job within the Presidency of the BiH. Why was it that you were appointed to this senior position within the government of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: The reason was because they knew that I had been on that job for about 20 years. Before I went to the Presidency, I was under-secretary of the government -- or rather, the Executive Council, which was then the government. And before that I always worked as a civil servant. Then I went to work in the Presidency -- or rather, as secretary of the council. This job, by its very nature, is the same like the -- that of under-secretary of the Executive Council of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps I'll be a bit immodest, but I should say that it's purely professional reasons that led to my appointment. That is one thing. And then another matter: There was not a single lawyer there, working there at the time -- well, this council will be discussed subsequently. So there wasn't anyone who could really handle the job except for this Nenad who, as I said, was very ill and had to go for this urgent operation, urgent surgery, and I really don't know how it all ended either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will look at various documents that relate to the job that you were appointed to. But before I ask you about that, could you give the Chamber an overview of the job that you performed for the Republika Srpska government in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: During the course of 1992 or later, I was not a member of government. That is to say that my appointment was not political. I was only in charge of organising the work of the government and carrying out the conclusions made at government sessions. By the very nature of this job, it is professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Give the Chamber some idea of the staff that you had at your disposal as the senior civil servant in the government.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, there was only one woman working there. She does not have a degree in law but she did have a university degree. And in addition to that, there were three employees with secondary-school education; a secretary and typists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was the name of the woman who had a university degree?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Draginja Antelj is her name now, but I cannot remember her maiden name right now, but her name now is Draginja Antelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What function did Rajka Stanisic perform?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Sometime in the beginning of May the government went to Pale -- in fact, she never worked for the government officially. Now, I'm not sure that she worked for the Presidency or the president of the Assembly, I'm not quite sure now what she did, because we were separated, physically. Say, we were 30 kilometres away, and there was such a lot of work to be done. I can show you all the regulations that we had to work on and that we did finish. I don't want to be immodest but I think that I took part in at least 80 per cent of the regulations that were published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. Everybody knows that my working hours were 18 a day. So I channeled my activities in terms of the government conclusions and carrying them out. I can't remember now exactly, but I think that at that time in 1992 about 90 government sessions were held. And believe it or not, at some sessions there would be about 50 items on the agenda. It was an enormous job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, after two or three lines on Rajko Stanisic, the witness continued with totally different subjects. If that is, of course, what you wanted to elicit from him, then I was wrong in stopping him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps could you take a bit more control there as well. I mean, you see after the fourth or the fifth line that, apart from the distance, then he starts telling about his own functions, which is not your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Although it was a question I asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but for the Chamber to follow the testimony, we'd rather not combine questions and answers somewhere on the transcript and rather have them in logical order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you were first appointed government secretary, where was the government physically located?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: For a very short period of time, about ten days, it was in the Kikinda building, and then the government moved from the Bistrica Hotel in Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did it move there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Because -- well, the government did not even have elementary conditions for work in Kikinda. There wasn't even a proper meeting room, and I think that the telephones weren't working either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So it's right, to confirm this, that the government moved to Jahorina in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of May, but I cannot exactly recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you were appointed to the job, were members of the government in place?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed to the job - excuse me - I think that at that moment there were three or four members of the government, with the Prime Minister at the head of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We know that the Prime Minister was Branko Djeric. To what extent did your job involve liaising with him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: By the very nature of this job, I had frequent contact with the Prime Minister because, in agreement with the ministers in charge who had been appointed in the meantime, he made proposals, and I agreed with him when the session -- or rather, sessions would be held and what items would be on the agenda. Then after the government sessions, I would make the minutes, he would have a look at the minutes, and then we'd agree on its implementation; namely, those materials that had to be published. If some of these materials were regulations passed by the government, then they would be prepared for publication in the Official Gazette. But if it was laws and other documents that had to be adopted by the Assembly, then we would make appropriate proposals and send them to the Assembly for discussion, for a parliamentary debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How often would you meet or liaise with the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I've already said that there were about 95 sessions during the course of 1992. Some sessions involved agendas of over 40 items. If all of that were to be taken into account, it seems that there was a government session held once a week. And that would mean that we were in touch at least twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want you to obviously try and paint a picture here. How close was your office to his?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a big hotel. As far as I know, it can take about 300 to 400 tourists. I think I never entered his room, but we had these big meeting rooms where we held our sessions, and that's where we usually had meetings when we needed to agree on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent did your job involve liaison with the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I never, well, had any contacts with the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did that go for all the members of the Presidency; you had no contact with them at all?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it could be said that I did not have any official contacts, but then whether I came across people like, say, the late Nikola Koljevic, if that's what you mean by contact with the Presidency, too, then there were contacts. But as for official contacts with the Presidency, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, it's apparent from the documents we've seen already that you knew Mrs. Plavsic well because she had been the president of the council to which you had previously been the secretary.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: Correct. I knew Mrs. Plavsic very well because we worked together in the Presidency, together with Mr. Koljevic. And we prepared sessions of the Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order. Sometimes we had consultations for sessions of the Presidency, too, if they were not held within the context of meetings of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Radovan Karadzic? To what extent did you have dealings with him after you had become government secretary?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember I ever had any contact with Radovan Karadzic. I had no need and I had no contact. I didn't know him either. I didn't know him personally until I came to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about Momcilo Krajisnik? Had you met him prior to your arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO LAKIC
utterances.text: No, never. I didn't know Momcilo Krajisnik. I don't think I ever had any personal contact with him. I only knew him from the media, when sessions of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock, and I have a small matter to raise procedurally. If you would find a suitable moment -- whether this would be a suitable moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, we'll stop for the day. Is my impression correct that you feel more at ease than you felt in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any beginning is difficult. I said at the very beginning that I felt uneasy because this is the first time I am a witness. So my behaviour is logical, and what the Honourable President said, that I was speaking slowly, I was told to speak slowly because this is being recorded, simultaneously interpreted, and so on. Secondly, I wasn't sure, when questions were being put to me, whether I was supposed to look at the Judge or to look at the person who was putting questions to me, so there was a kind of confusion that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that, and I also got the impression that you feel better at ease now. And looking at the interpreters, I think that your speed of speech is such that they can easily follow you, so just take the speed you find comfortable, as I hope you do by now. Mr. Lakic, we'll continue tomorrow. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give in the days to come. Mr. Lakic, we'd like to see you back tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, in this same courtroom. Would you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence responded on the 8th of March to the omnibus order of the 2nd of March. I'd like to address that issue. The Trial Chamber has yet to decide on the admission of certain items in light of the Defence response of 8th of March, 2006, to the omnibus order of the 2nd of March. Firstly, considering that the Defence, in its response of the 2nd [sic] of March, noted that it does not wish to have item D84 translated, this provisionally admitted item is no longer eligible for admission and the exhibit number D84 is now available for assignment to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did we use the word "wish," Your Honour? That certainly was -- if I used that word in drafting the motion, I certainly didn't intend it. It would not have that meaning in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that you are not able to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I correct what I said. In your response of the 2nd [sic] of March, you noted that it was not able to provide the Chamber with a translation of D84 and that therefore this provisionally admitted item is no longer eligible, because the consequences are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Secondly, considering that there has been no objection to the admission of the items marked D133 and D138, the Chamber hereby admits D133 and D138 in evidence. Thirdly, regarding item D114, the Chamber requests the Defence to submit the English version of D114 by the 20th of March. Fourthly, regarding item D123, the Chamber hereby grants an extension of ten days to the Defence to submit the item. The new deadline for submission is Monday, the 27th of March. Finally, regarding item D139, the Chamber regrets, having stated in its omnibus order, that it had given the Defence guidance on the question of its admission. In fact, we had not done so. The Chamber hereby requests the Defence to submit the CD of the interview and a B/C/S version of the transcript of the interview to the Chamber by Monday, the 27th of March. This concludes the Chamber's comments on the Defence response of the 8th of March. Additionally, the Chamber would like to address the Defence regarding the items provisionally marked with Prosecution exhibit numbers during the examination of Witness Savkic. The Chamber requests the Defence to inform the Chamber at the start of tomorrow's hearing, firstly, which, if any, of the Savkic items is still -- it still opposes; and, secondly, if one or more of these items are still being opposed by the Defence, any final submissions the Defence might have in support of its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear. Your Honour, the Chamber will still need to fix a date for arguments so far as the Poplasen exhibits are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would help me enormously if we were given a little bit of time in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we now set a date at this very moment, will that already give you some additional time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It will bring a smile to my face, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Radojko list has now been distributed between the parties so that we can deal with that efficiently, not at this moment, but soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
